# NearEats

> Find restaurants, cafes and bars near you — with what's open right now, diet options, step-free access, real walking time and one-tap directions. One-time $1.99, no subscription.

NearEats is an iPhone app that finds places to eat and drink around you and shows the details that decide where you actually go: whether a place is open right now (or closing in 25 minutes), whether it does vegan, halal, kosher or gluten-free, whether you can get in without steps, how long the walk really is, and whether it takes cards. It merges OpenStreetMap and Apple Maps so a venue found in both appears once with the best details from each. There is no account and no sign-up. It is a directory of facts, not a review platform — it has no ratings, reviews or user photos, because no open data source provides them honestly.

## Key Facts

- Platform: iOS (iPhone, iOS 18+)
- Pricing: $1.99 one-time purchase on the App Store. No subscription, no in-app purchases, no ads, no free tier
- Data sources: OpenStreetMap (Overpass API) and Apple Maps (MapKit), merged and de-duplicated
- Privacy: no account, no sign-up, no email. Saved and visited places stay on the device; search results are cached locally for 30 days. Anonymous usage analytics including session replay are sent to PostHog (EU) — see https://neareats.12f.dk/privacy-policy.html. Nothing is sold
- Languages: 49
- Developer: 12F ApS, Denmark (https://12f.dk/)
- Website: https://neareats.12f.dk/
- App Store: https://apps.apple.com/us/app/neareats-restaurant-finder/id6754101006

## Features

- Restaurants, cafes and bars — three categories, switched with one control
- Clustered map with a synced list; tap a pin to highlight the venue
- Smart opening status read against the current time: "Open now", "Closes in 25 min", "Opens at 17:00"
- Open-late filter for the evening question
- Diet options per venue: vegan, vegetarian, halal, kosher, gluten-free, dairy-free, organic
- Accessibility: wheelchair access and accessible toilets, including a red warning when a venue is NOT accessible
- Warning badges for decision-critical negatives, shown ahead of the positives: cash only, not wheelchair accessible
- Amenities: outdoor seating, Wi-Fi, takeaway, delivery, drive-through, dog-friendly, family-friendly, air conditioning, microbrewery, fireplace
- Michelin and Bib Gourmand award badges where a venue has one
- Route-accurate walking time, not straight-line distance
- "Surprise me" — one tap picks a venue for you
- Search and filter by name, cuisine or feature
- "Been here" journal to mark places worth returning to
- One-tap directions, plus the venue's website and phone number
- 30-day on-device cache for speed and poor connections
- Dark mode, Dynamic Type and VoiceOver support

## What NearEats deliberately does not have

- No ratings, reviews, star scores or user photos — no free data source provides them honestly, so the app shows facts instead
- No account, sign-up or login
- No ads, and no paid placement: no venue can pay to appear higher in a list
- No subscription

## Blog

Practical guidance on finding somewhere good to eat, published at https://neareats.12f.dk/blog/ (RSS: https://neareats.12f.dk/feed.xml).

- [Why review scores are a bad way to choose a restaurant when travelling](https://neareats.12f.dk/blog/why-review-scores-are-a-bad-way-to-choose-a-restaurant-when-travelling/) — travel-tips, 2026-08-27. Why a review score of 4.4 means something different in Copenhagen than in Naples, and why sorting by rating while travelling tends to surface the places that optimise for reviews rather than the places that are actually good.
- [Where to eat late in an unfamiliar city: the method that works](https://neareats.12f.dk/blog/where-to-eat-late-in-an-unfamiliar-city/) — eating-out, 2026-08-27. A practical method for finding food late in a city you do not know: how closing times actually work (kitchen close versus door close, split hours, seasonal changes, public holidays), the six venue types that stay open late by structure rather than by luck, and the ten-minute pre-walk checks — map apps, a phone call, hotel and bar counters — that settle it before you set off.
- [Wheelchair access in restaurants: the questions that settle the visit](https://neareats.12f.dk/blog/wheelchair-access-in-restaurants-the-questions-that-settle-the-visit/) — dietary, 2026-08-27. A practical checklist for someone who uses a wheelchair (or is choosing a venue for someone who does) planning a restaurant visit in an unfamiliar city: the two failure points — the threshold and the table — the door-width check that settles most of the risk before the visit, the three questions to ask the venue by phone or message and what each answer tells you, the honest limits of online wheelchair-access data, the toilet as the part people forget to plan for, and what to do when the answer to any of it is no.
- [Kosher food away from home: planning without a community to ask](https://neareats.12f.dk/blog/kosher-food-away-from-home-planning/) — dietary, 2026-08-27. A practical guide to eating kosher in a city where no one is around who can just tell you the answer: which supervision systems exist, what a certification label actually covers (and when it stops covering — most notably during passover), the questions that settle a restaurant before you sit down, how to plan the first meal of a trip, and the honest limits of online checking.
- [Moving to a new city: finding your regular spots in the first month](https://neareats.12f.dk/blog/first-month-in-a-new-city-finding-your-regular-spots/) — city-guides, 2026-08-27. A practical method for building your regular eating places during the first month in a new city: how to scope the search by walking distance instead of app radius, which venue types make good regulars and which are built for one visits, how to vet a candidate place in a single visit by asking for the second or third option on the menu, how to check opening hours, prices, and reservations before you commit to a spot, and the honest limits of crowd-sourced data when your new neighbourhood is thin.
- [How to find a place open late in a city you don't know](https://neareats.12f.dk/blog/finding-a-place-open-late-in-a-city-you-dont-know/) — eating-out, 2026-08-27. A practical method for eating out late in a city you do not know: how closing times work in the main cuisines and city types (kitchen close, split hours, public holidays), what the gaps in the evening mean, which venue types genuinely stay open late, and the ten-minute check you can do before walking, plus the honest limits of any app's opening-hours data.
- [How to find halal food while travelling, without relying on guesswork](https://neareats.12f.dk/blog/find-halal-food-while-travelling/) — dietary, 2026-08-27. A practical method for finding reliably halal food in a city you don't know.
- [How to find a decent coffee in a city full of chains](https://neareats.12f.dk/blog/find-a-decent-coffee-in-a-city-full-of-chains/) — eating-out, 2026-08-27. Practical guidance for finding genuinely good coffee in a city with lots of chain coffee shops.
- [Eating out with a severe food allergy abroad: what to check](https://neareats.12f.dk/blog/eating-out-with-a-severe-food-allergy-abroad/) — dietary, 2026-08-27. A practical guide for someone with a severe (IgE-mediated) food allergy eating in an unfamiliar city: why the reaction timeline changes the decision, the pre-visit questions that separate a kitchen that has built a system from one that will try to be careful, the dish types that are lower risk by construction, the written-word and disclosure-labelling shortcuts, the epinephrine logistics, and the honest limit that no amount of checking makes a shared kitchen safe in the absolute sense.
- [Eating gluten-free abroad: what to check before you sit down](https://neareats.12f.dk/blog/eating-gluten-free-abroad-what-to-check/) — dietary, 2026-08-27. A practical guide to eating gluten-free in an unfamiliar city: which menu items are safe by construction and which look safe but are cooked with flour in the pan, the language shortcuts for asking about gluten and cross-contamination, and how to verify a place's gluten-free capability before you sit down.
- [Food allergies abroad: the phrases and checks that actually work](https://neareats.12f.dk/blog/allergies-abroad-the-phrases-and-checks-that-actually-work/) — dietary, 2026-08-27. A practical guide to communicating a food allergy in a restaurant that does not speak your language: why a written three-line card beats translation, the process questions that separate a kitchen with a real system from one that will try to be careful, how allergen labelling laws differ by country and what that means for how hard to lean on them, and the honest limit that no phrase, card or law turns a shared kitchen into a guarantee.
